newsitem.title: USA: Administration urges rise in U.S. foreign spending.
newsitem.headline: Administration urges rise in U.S. foreign spending.

text.p: The Clinton administration, saying future events in the former Soviet Union posed the most serious threat to the United States, on Thursday proposed raising foreign spending to reassert U.S. world leadership.
Following years of declines in its international affairs budget, the White House asked Congress for a seven percent rise in 1998 to nearly $19.5 billion.

Newly appointed Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told a news conference it was "a plan of action for protecting America's vital interests, a plan that funds not the extravagant, but the essential".

Most of the increase came from a $1.1 billion rise in foreign aid, including a 44 percent hike -- to $900 million -- in aid to former Soviet states that would include a new $528 million programme to be known as Partnership for Freedom.

The request also contained details of an already publicised plan to help pay arrears of more than $1 billion of United Nations dues by seeking a one-off advance appropriation of $921 million to become available in 1999.
Although foreign affairs accounts for little more than one percent of President Bill Clinton's $1.69 trillion budget, few issues raise more hackles in the Republican-led Congress.
But the request received a cautious welcome from New York Republican Benjamin Gilman, chairman of the House of Representatives International Relations Committee.

Gilman said in a statement that while he did not endorse everything in it, "with our new secretaries of state and defence, I think we can forge a bipartisan consensus with the administration on the basis of this budget request."

The budget request said a less orderly world created new challenges to U.S. security, and this was no time to fall back into "isolationism and protectionism" by failing to fund Washington's mission of global leadership.

It said that "perhaps the most serious national security threat facing the nation today hinges on the course of events over the next few years in the New Independent States of the former Soviet Union".

The large vote for opponents of Boris Yeltsin in Russia's 1996 presidential election, due to Moscow's "severe economic distress", served a warning that it was "absolutely critical" to back democratic reform and free markets in the region.
Officials said that Partnership for Freedom was aimed at promoting investment, trade and anti-crime programmes.

Richard Morningstar, chief coordinator of aid to former Soviet states, said one idea was an initiative to help development of local banks, offering them guarantees on a shared basis that might help promote U.S. exports.
The proposed allocation to support the Middle East peace process -- most of it military and civil aid to Israel and Egypt -- was increased slightly over 1997 to $5.3 billion.
Over half the $100 million increase was due to an initial U.S. contribution to a planned Middle East development bank.
Albright said the aim of paying off arrears to the United Nations and other international bodies was to ensure continued American leadership in them and promote U.N. reform.
"We cannot hope to lead that reform effort if we do not pay what we owe. As in poker, to have a seat at the table, we have to put chips in the pot," she said.
Officials stressed that the money would only be paid over if Washington and the United Nations agreed on cuts in annual U.S. dues -- a key demand of the body's many foes in Congress.

The budget also proposed an eight percent rise -- to $230 million -- in funding for the State Department's narcotics and anti-crime programmes. Most of the increase would go to programmes in Peru, it said.
